chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Abbas ibn Musa from Yunus from Sulayman ibn Salim said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who hired a worker for a specified amount of expenses and dirhams, on the condition that he send him to a land. When he arrived, a man from his companions invited him to his house for a month or two, and he would obtain from him what would suffice him from the expenses of the employer. The worker looked at what was being spent on him in the month; if he did not invite him, he compensated him with that which the inviter was giving. Whose property is that compensation? Is it the property of the worker or the property of the employer? He (peace be upon him) said: 'If it is in the interest of the employer, it is from his property, and otherwise it is upon the worker.'

And [asked] about a man who hired a worker for specified expenses without specifying anything else, on the condition that he send him to a land. As for the expenses of the worker from washing clothes or the bathhouse, who bears it? He said: 'It is upon the employer.'
ai.seo_question: Who bears the cost of incidental expenses and third-party gifts when an employer sends a worker on a mission?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Rida (AS) establishes the principle of *maslaha* (interest/benefit) in determining ownership of incidental gains during employment, reflecting the Shia juristic emphasis on fairness in contractual obligations. It clarifies that while basic sustenance and hygiene costs are the employer's responsibility, any surplus or third-party benefits accrue to the employer only if they serve the employer's specific interest, otherwise remaining with the worker. This ruling underscores the detailed application of *fiqh al-mu'amalat* in classical Shia jurisprudence regarding agency and labor contracts.
